messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 48
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Social Ministry Worker
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening accident
- Pcl5: 57

Margaret is forty-eight years old, single, and has worked for the past eighteen years as a social ministry coordinator for a church-based nonprofit in a mid-sized Midwestern city. She spends her days visiting homebound parishioners, organizing food drives, and sitting with families in crisis. Her work has always felt like a calling—something she was put on earth to do. That changed on a Tuesday in late November, two years ago.

She was driving home from a rural outreach visit just after dusk. The rain had turned to freezing drizzle, and the two-lane highway was glazed. She remembers the headlights coming toward her—how they seemed to swerve slowly, almost gently, into her lane. There was no time to brake. The impact crumpled the driver’s side door, snapped her seatbelt in half, and sent her car into a ditch. She woke up in the ICU three days later with a shattered pelvis, four broken ribs, and a traumatic brain injury that wiped out the memory of the crash itself—but not the feeling. She still feels the metal folding around her. She feels the cold. She feels the stop.

The physical recovery took months. She moved back into her small apartment and learned to walk again with a cane she hated. But it was the other things that began to hollow her out. She stopped driving entirely, even as a passenger. She told her supervisor she could do all her visits by phone, and for a while that worked. Then she started skipping meetings. She would find herself frozen in the grocery store parking lot, heart pounding, sure she could feel the crash coming again even though she was standing still. She started checking her rearview mirror obsessively from the passenger seat of any car she was in—and she only ever rides with her sister now, and only during daylight, and only on streets she knows.

At work, she can’t sit through a full counseling session with a parishioner who talks about grief or loss. She finds her mind drifting to the shatter of glass, the smell of antifreeze. She interrupts people. She tells them they’ll be fine, then ends the call. She has stopped visiting the hospital altogether because the antiseptic smell triggers a wave of nausea and a sense of being trapped. Her supervisor has noticed, but Margaret says she’s still recovering from the accident, which is true—but not the whole truth.

At night, she dreams of the sleeting rain and the blinding lights. She wakes up gasping, confused, sometimes crying, sometimes just staring at the ceiling until dawn. She has started drinking a glass of wine before bed to slow the thoughts, and sometimes two. She doesn’t go out with friends anymore. She told them she gets tired early, which is also true, but the real reason is that being in any crowd makes her feel vulnerable, as if danger is hiding in plain sight. She scans every room for exits. She startles when someone touches her shoulder from behind.

She used to pray every morning. Now she finds herself angry at God—not openly, but in a quiet, buried way. She thinks about the families she used to comfort, and she wonders how she ever had the nerve to tell them everything would be okay when clearly nothing is okay. She feels guilty for not being able to return to full ministry, guilty for being a burden to her sister, guilty for the driver of the other car (who died at the scene, though she knows logically it wasn’t her fault). She replays the seconds before the crash over and over, even though she doesn’t remember them. She imagines what she could have done differently. She cannot stop.

These days, Margaret wears a thin silver cross that her mother gave her, but she rarely touches it. She sits at her desk in the church office, looking at the calendar of upcoming visits, and feels a weight in her chest that won’t lift. She is still a social ministry worker, but she feels like a ghost of the person she was. The accident ended, but something inside her never pulled out of the ditch.
